## What compaction does with them

Compaction (`RewriteDataFiles`) rewrites the *data* files, not deletes. Concretely:

1. It plans a scan and groups tasks by partition, keeping only partitions with more than one data file; nothing to rewrite otherwise (`BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.execute`, core/.../actions/BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java:246-256). Only reads data files, so `.ignoreResiduals()` on the scan (line 233) — the delete-filtering happened before this.
2. `rewriteDataForTasks` (line 276) reads the old files (applying whatever deletes apply to them) and writes new compacted data files containing only the live rows — the commas of deleted rows are dropped.
3. It commits with `table.newRewrite()`: marks the old data files deleted and adds the new ones — `rewriteFiles.deleteFile(dataFile)` / `addFile(dataFile)` (BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java:331-346).

What compaction does *not* do by default: it does **not** carry delete files into the rewritten snapshot. It only swaps data files (BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java:333-339). After compaction, the rewritten data files already have the deletes baked out as physical row removal, and the delete files are left tracked but applying to superseded/expired data files; they get cleaned up later — position deletes by `RewritePositionDeletesCommitManager`/`RemoveDanglingDeleteFilesAction`, and orphaned delete files by `RemoveDanglingDeleteFilesAction`. Since deletes only apply to older data files in the same partition (spec.md:1088), a delete whose target data file has been compacted away no longer matches anything.

Compaction has one subtle correctness lever worth calling out: `useStartingSequenceNumber`. By default the rew shuffled files get the new snapshot's sequence number, which would make them *newer* than newer equality deletes and thus incorrectly escape them. To preserve correct delete semantics, compaction can instead stamp rewritten files with the sequence number of the snapshot at compaction start, `rewriteFiles.dataSequenceNumber(sequenceNumber)` (BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java:341-344), so the rewritten files keep their data age and don't mask newer equality deletes. The javadoc explains this is "to avoid commit conflicts with updates that add newer equality deletes" (BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java:204-208).
